title: API Authentication Methods
description: Explore common API authentication patterns including API keys, Basic Auth, OAuth 2.0, and JWT, and learn how to choose the right approach for your system.

data.text: Authentication ensures that only authorized clients can access your API. The right authentication method depends on your threat model, client types, and how much user context the API needs. In interviews, being able to compare authentication approaches and explain their trade-offs shows security awareness and design maturity. A poor choice can expose user data, leak credentials, or make revocation impossible without downtime.

API keys are simple shared secrets passed in a header or query parameter. They are easy to implement and widely supported by gateways, but they lack user-level context and are hard to rotate safely. API keys are best suited for machine-to-machine integrations where individual user identity is not required. Because they grant access indefinitely until revoked, leaking an API key can be catastrophic for platforms that do not enforce IP restrictions or usage quotas.

data.title: API Key Usage
data.content: Pass the key in a custom header to keep it out of logs and browser history.

data.text: Basic Auth sends a username and password encoded with Base64 in the Authorization header. It is defined in RFC 7617 and supported by almost every HTTP client. However, it must always be used over HTTPS because Base64 is not encryption. Basic Auth is simple but does not scale well to third-party integrations or fine-grained permissions. It also forces clients to store credentials, which increases the blast radius of a client-side compromise.

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that lets clients obtain limited access tokens without sharing credentials. It supports multiple grant types including authorization code for web apps, client credentials for services, and refresh tokens for long-lived sessions. OAuth 2.0 is more complex to implement than API keys, but it provides strong delegation, scoping, and revocation capabilities. For third-party integrations, OAuth 2.0 is almost always the right choice because it limits the damage if a token is compromised.

data.title: OAuth 2.0 vs OpenID Connect
data.text: OAuth 2.0 handles authorization, while OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds identity on top of OAuth 2.0. Use OIDC when you need to know who the user is, not just what they are allowed to do.

JSON Web Tokens are compact, signed tokens that carry claims about the user or client. They are often used with OAuth 2.0 or as standalone session tokens. Because JWTs are self-contained, servers can validate them without querying a database, which reduces latency. The trade-off is that revoking a JWT before expiration requires additional infrastructure such as blocklists or short token lifetimes. JWTs also grow in size as you add claims, which can increase header overhead on every request.

items.question: Should I roll my own authentication?
items.answer: No. Use proven libraries and frameworks. Custom authentication often introduces subtle vulnerabilities in token handling, password storage, and timing attacks.

items.question: How do I secure API keys?
items.answer: Store keys in secret managers, rotate them regularly, use separate keys for production and development, and revoke keys immediately if they leak.

data.title: Takeaway
points: API keys are simple but lack user context and strong revocation.
Basic Auth is acceptable only over HTTPS.
OAuth 2.0 provides the strongest delegation and scoping model.
JWT reduces database lookups but requires careful revocation strategy.
data.takeaway: Match the authentication method to your threat model and user experience requirements.
